explain.say: Scaffolding is a temporary steel frame that lets builders work safely at height. It starts on the ground, with base plates on timber boards so the legs do not sink into soft ground.

explain.say: Upright tubes called standards are linked by horizontal tubes called ledgers and transoms, clamped together with steel couplers into a grid. The standards carry the weight of workers and materials down to the base.

faq.a: Scaffolding is a frame of steel tubes clamped into a grid, stiffened with diagonal braces and tied into the building. Base plates spread its weight on the ground.

faq.q: Why does scaffolding stand on base plates and boards?
faq.a: Each leg carries a concentrated load that could punch into soft ground. A steel base plate on a timber sole board spreads the load over a wider area.

faq.q: Why does scaffolding have diagonal poles?
faq.a: Diagonal braces turn the rectangles of the frame into triangles, which cannot change shape. Without them, the frame could lean over and collapse sideways.
Ties are fixings that connect the scaffold to the building at regular intervals. They stop the tall, narrow frame toppling outward or being blown over by wind.
asks: Why is scaffolding fixed to the building?

faq.q: How is scaffolding made safe for workers?
faq.a: Platforms are fully boarded, with guardrails and toe boards along the edges to stop people and tools falling, and the scaffold is inspected regularly by trained people.
asks: What stops people falling off scaffolding?

facts: Standard steel scaffold tube has an outside diameter of 48.3 millimetres, so fittings from different suppliers fit.
Tall scaffolds are tied into the building at regular intervals to resist wind and stop them toppling.

quiz.say: A scaffold frame of rectangular bays sways sideways when pushed. What should be added?
quiz.why: Diagonal braces create triangles, which make the frame rigid.

wrong.1: Boards add weight but do not stop the rectangles folding sideways.
wrong.2: Paint protects against rust but adds no stiffness.
